title: Bad Faith and Self-Deception
text:
Jean-Paul Sartre used the phrase 'bad faith' to describe the habit of pretending that our choices are determined by circumstances or by our nature. A waiter who performs his role too perfectly, Sartre observed, is acting out an identity rather than living freely. Such self-deception may bring comfort, but it hides the anguish that accompanies genuine freedom.

Sartre did not condemn all roles, however. The problem arises only when a person treats a role as a fixed essence that excuses their decisions. Recognising this illusion is itself an act of freedom, because it forces the individual to acknowledge that they are responsible for who they become.

questions.text: What did Sartre describe as 'bad faith'?
options: The habit of pretending choices are determined by circumstances or nature
A refusal to accept payment for work
Loyalty to a fixed set of religious laws

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what is the problem?
options: Treating a role as a fixed essence that excuses one's decisions
Having no social roles at all

questions.text: Why does the passage say that recognising this illusion is an act of freedom?
options: Because it forces the individual to acknowledge their responsibility for who they become
Because it allows people to escape all roles
Because it removes the anguish of choice
Because it proves that circumstances determine identity

questions.text: What is implied about the waiter in the first paragraph?
options: He is living freely and authentically
He is acting out an identity rather than choosing it
He has no understanding of his work
He is unaware of any social expectations

vocabulary.definition: a false belief or a misleading appearance
the fundamental nature that makes something what it is
having the duty to answer for one's own actions

paragraph_translations: Jean-Paul Sartre użył określenia „zła wiara”, aby opisać nawyk udawania, że nasze wybory są determinowane przez okoliczności lub naszą naturę. Kelner, który wykonuje swoją rolę zbyt doskonale, jak zauważył Sartre, odgrywa tożsamość zamiast żyć wolnie. Takie samooszukiwanie się może przynosić pocieszenie, ale ukrywa udrękę, która towarzyszy prawdziwej wolności.

Sartre nie potępiał jednak wszystkich ról. Problem pojawia się dopiero wtedy, gdy człowiek traktuje rolę jako stałą istotę, która usprawiedliwia jego decyzje. Rozpoznanie tej złudzenia jest już samo w sobie aktem wolności, ponieważ zmusza jednostkę do uznania, że jest odpowiedzialna za to, kim się staje.
